title: Rereading chapters 5–8
hook: reread the fool, the wise, the venerable, the thousands
tomorrow: why would a book print the same verse twice, one phrase changed?

segments.voice: Yesterday the reread began with the twin verses, earnestness, thought and flowers: new verses in old pages. Same book, a different reader. Now the next four chapters, and the first one is about fools.
screen: `NEW VERSES IN OLD PAGES.` → `NOW, THE FOOL.`

segments.voice: The pencil marks are what get you. A paperback comes down off the shelf after a few years, and there they are: underlines, a star, a word in the margin in handwriting that's yours, only younger. Most of the marks still make sense. Then one star sits next to a line that now reads like it was written about you, and not kindly. That's what happens on a second pass through the Dhammapada's next four chapters: the fool, the wise, the worthy one, the thousands. The first time, the fool chapter reads like a list of other people. The second time, one verse turns around and looks back.
screen: `THE OLD PENCIL MARKS.` → `ONE STAR STINGS.` → `THE FOOL, THE WISE, THE WORTHY, THE THOUSANDS.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in Max Müller's translation: “The fool who knows his foolishness, is wise at least so far. But a fool who thinks himself wise, he is called a fool indeed.” Read once, that's a clever line. Reread, it's a door. By this verse, the fool isn't the person who gets things wrong. Everyone does. The fool is the one who can't see it. So the wince at an old mark is good news: seeing the foolishness is already being wise, at least so far. Then the chapter on the wise gives two pictures of where that leads. The wise are like a solid rock that wind can't shake, steady under blame and praise. And after hearing the teaching, they grow calm like a deep, still lake. The chapter on the worthy one, the person who has reached the goal, says their path is hard to trace, like birds in the air. Then the thousands. One word of sense that brings quiet is better than a thousand empty ones. And the line people remember: “If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors.” On a first read, that's a slogan. On a reread, after the fool verse, it has a job. The battle with yourself starts with noticing. Wiser now doesn't mean finished. It means the same page looks different, because the reader has changed.
screen: `THE FOOL WHO KNOWS IT IS WISE SO FAR.` · `THE ROCK AND THE STILL LAKE.` · `ONE WORD OF SENSE.` · `CONQUER YOURSELF.` · then, large: `WISER NOW.`

segments.voice: Choose one verse from today's four chapters: the fool who knows it, the rock, the still lake, or the one who conquers himself. Copy it by hand onto paper, slowly, word by word, while the sit runs. Then mark it the way you'd mark it now: a star, a word in the margin, today's date.
Rereading chapters 5 to 8: the fool, the wise, the worthy one and the thousands, read a second time. On a reread, the verse that stings can be the one that helps.
The line to take with you: wiser now, and the wince is part of it. Four more chapters, reread.

fork.setup: your little brother rereads the essay he was so proud of last year and groans that it's awful. what would the fool verse say to him?
options: seeing what's weak in it now is already a step toward wise.
stop rereading old work; looking back only stirs up regret.
the essay was fine; wise people never criticize their past.
fork.reveal: the fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least so far. the groan is a sign his eye has grown.

original.note: Pali: fool, and also a child; the fifth chapter is the Bālavagga, the chapter on the fool.

chat.says: pulling portfolio pieces and found my freshman sketchbook. it's SO bad. embarrassing. should i just toss it?
options: keep it. wincing means you can see now what you couldn't then.
toss it. wise people don't dwell on old mistakes; they move on.
keep it, but don't judge it. old work and new are equally good.
chat.meaning: Dhammapada 63: the fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least so far. Seeing the old mistakes is the sign of growth.
